decisions.decision: The board effectively agreed to stop the blending water-quality tests, since the superintendent's conversation with MassDEP established that blending will not be accepted as a long-term compliance method and every individual well must pass PFAS limits on its own.
The board agreed to ask Townsend, in writing, for a price to supply the district's average and peak daily water demand as an alternative to building a treatment plant.

The board agreed that one commissioner (Bill/Mr. Rekkey) could meet informally with MassDEP for informational purposes only, not as an official board representative and with no decision-making authority.

The superintendent will obtain quotes for cleaning the Keings well and the Lancaster/Hickory Hills wells so the board can consider a special meeting to appropriate funds, likely scheduled for a low-usage period such as winter.
The board agreed not to charge a new connection fee to the food pantry's trailers because a pre-existing connection to the property already existed; usage costs would still apply.
For the package store project, the district will waive a connection fee only if the existing connection is shut off at the main; otherwise standard individual connection fees apply.

minutes.headline: DEP says every well must meet PFAS limits alone by 2029; blending won't count, forcing plant-vs-buy choice
minutes.summary: The Water Commissioners reviewed warrants and minutes, then spent most of the meeting on MassDEP's PFAS ("PFOA/PFOS") requirements, learning that each individual well must independently meet the state limit by 2029 and that blending water from multiple sources will not be accepted as a permanent compliance strategy. The board discussed two paths forward -- building a treatment plant or purchasing water from Townsend -- without deciding between them, and separately took up bacteria failures at several wells, a proposal to fund cleaning of the Keings and Lancaster wells at a future special meeting, and connection-fee questions for the food pantry and a package store project.

what_happened.line: MassDEP told the district every well must meet PFAS limits on its own by 2029, and blending from multiple sources will not count as compliance, forcing a choice between a treatment plant or buying water elsewhere.
The board agreed to ask the town of Townsend in writing for a price to supply the district's water demand as an alternative to building a treatment plant, without choosing between the two paths.
Several wells are currently failing bacteria tests, prompting emergency chlorine dosing at one well.
The superintendent will gather quotes to clean the Keings and Lancaster wells and bring them to a future special meeting for the board to consider funding.
The board waived a new connection fee for the food pantry's relocation, citing a pre-existing connection, and set a conditional waiver for a package store project.

why_it_matters: Whichever path the district picks for PFAS compliance -- a treatment plant or buying water from Townsend -- is likely to show up on residents' water rates, and the board has not yet chosen or costed either option.
Bacteria failures at multiple wells and the emergency chlorine dosing concern the safety of water currently reaching customers' taps.
How the district treats connection fees on existing hookups, as decided here for the food pantry and a package store, sets a precedent other applicants may point to.
